## [ISSUE] Equal order() values turn a former fail-fast misconfiguration into a silent, classpath-order-dependent choice

**Severity:** MEDIUM - a FIPS deployment that also has `keycloak-crypto-default` on the classpath can silently use non-FIPS BouncyCastle

### The Problem

```java
List<CryptoProvider> foundProviders = StreamSupport.stream(ServiceLoader.load(CryptoProvider.class, classLoader).spliterator(), false)
        .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
...
return foundProviders.get(0);
```

Before this PR, `detectProvider` threw `IllegalStateException("Multiple crypto providers loaded ...")` when more than one provider was found. The PR removes that check and picks the one with the highest `order()`. But the three server providers all return the same value:

- `DefaultCryptoProvider.order()` -> 200
- `FIPS1402Provider.order()` -> 200 (and `Fips1402StrictCryptoProvider` inherits it)
- `WildFlyElytronProvider.order()` -> 200

Only `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (100) is different. When two of the 200-providers are both visible, `Stream.sorted` is stable, so the winner is whichever one `ServiceLoader` finds first. That is the classpath/jar order. The only trace is a `debug`-level "Ignored crypto providers" line.

### Theory / Proof

- `ServiceLoader` iteration order follows `ClassLoader.getResources` order, and the javadoc does not guarantee it. `Stream.sorted` is stable for ordered streams, so ties keep that order.
- FIPS and default at the same time is a real configuration. `testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/pom.xml` (profile `auth-server-quarkus-embedded`) excludes `keycloak-crypto-fips1402` from `keycloak-junit5` because the two conflict. Before this PR the conflict caused a hard failure. After it, the result depends on which jar comes first.
- `CryptoIntegration.init(...)` is still how the provider is chosen in `KeycloakApplication`, in admin-cli `Globals`, in the testsuite `CryptoInitRule`, and now in `AuthzClient`. Quarkus is not affected because it calls `setProvider` explicitly.

### What happens today vs. what will break

Today every shipped distribution bundles only one server crypto module, so there are no ties. If an application or a test classpath has both `keycloak-crypto-fips1402` and `keycloak-crypto-default` (for example through a transitive dependency), it used to fail at startup with a clear message. Now it starts, possibly with `DefaultCryptoProvider`, and nothing above debug level says so. That quietly breaks the FIPS guarantee.

### Research

The PR description says the goal is only to let the *client* provider step aside for a real provider. Other SPI-ordering schemes (for example Keycloak's own `ProviderFactory.order()` for default provider selection) either give distinct priorities or report ambiguity when priorities are equal.

### Recommendation

Keep the fail-fast behaviour when the top priority is tied, and only allow lower-priority providers to be ignored:

```java
CryptoProvider first = foundProviders.get(0);
if (foundProviders.size() > 1 && foundProviders.get(1).order() == first.order()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Multiple crypto providers with the same order " + first.order()
            + " loaded with the classLoader: " + classLoader + ". Available providers: " + foundProviders);
}
```

Alternatively, give FIPS a higher order than default (e.g. FIPS 300, default/elytron 200) so a FIPS jar always wins deterministically, and log the ignored providers at `info`/`warn` rather than `debug`.

## [GAP ANALYSIS] `order()` should be a default method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI

**Severity:** MEDIUM - source break for any external `CryptoProvider`, and a narrow runtime `AbstractMethodError` on mixed classpaths

### The Problem

```java
int order();
```

`order()` has no default body. The same interface already adds its newer methods as defaults, for example `default Stream<KeystoreFormat> getSupportedKeyStoreTypes()` (line 104) and `default String[] getSupportedRsaKeySizes()` (line 137). This new method breaks that pattern.

### Theory / Proof

- Source compatibility: any `CryptoProvider` implemented outside this repo no longer compiles against the new `keycloak-common`. That includes the copy of `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` that the PR description says will be synced to the separate `keycloak-client` repository.
- Runtime: `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` sorts with `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)`. With a single provider, `List.sort`/TimSort never calls the comparator, so nothing breaks. With two or more providers, calling `order()` on a class compiled against the old interface throws `java.lang.AbstractMethodError` (JLS 13.5.3). Before this PR, two or more providers already failed with `IllegalStateException`, so this does not break a setup that works today. It does affect exactly the new scenario this PR enables: the authz-client provider sitting next to a custom or older provider jar. There the user gets an `AbstractMethodError` from inside a comparator instead of a normal selection.

### What happens today vs. what will break

Every implementation in this repo overrides `order()`, so the build is green. Custom or out-of-repo `CryptoProvider` implementations stop compiling. If one of them was already compiled and ends up on a classpath with the authz-client provider, `AuthzClient.create(...)` throws `AbstractMethodError`.

### Research

Keycloak's own `ProviderFactory.order()` is a `default` method returning 0, and this interface already uses defaults for its later additions.

### Recommendation

```java
/**
 * Order of this provider. Higher number has preference over lower number when more providers are on the classpath.
 */
default int order() {
    return 0;
}
```

Keep the explicit overrides (200 / 100) in the providers touched by this PR.
kept.evidence: CryptoProvider.java:44 declares abstract `int order();`, while newer methods in the same interface are defaults (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes at :104, getSupportedRsaKeySizes at :137), so external implementations get a source break. The runtime AbstractMethodError is narrower than claimed: TimSort never calls the comparator for fewer than 2 elements, and 2 or more providers already threw IllegalStateException before this PR.

kept.claim: The test only checks that the new hand-written ASN.1 encoder and decoder are inverses of each other; it never checks that concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces the DER that the JCA verifier accepts (or equals the original signature), so symmetric encoder/decoder bugs would pass.
kept.evidence: ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:52-56 only checks rsConcat == rsConcat2 and never compares asn1Des with sign or passes it to verify. Line 42 uses KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC"), which defaults to P-256, so the ES512 test's DER stays under 128 bytes and the long-form length code (ASN1Encoder.java:67-79, ASN1Decoder.java:137-164) is never exercised.

An inner 0x80 gives an element truncated to its tag bytes, and readInteger then throws EOFException (an IOException) in readLength before read(-1) runs. The validator fuzzed 200k inputs and got only IOException or success.
